scope: Design-stage editorial descriptions for the 48 existing armament focus keys. English player-facing prose; 45–75 words each.

descriptions.armament_gaullist_a: The DMA's inherited arsenals and the new inter-service procurement system give the Republic a base for long production runs, but each new programme competes with social and regional investment. This route directs capital toward French-designed armoured vehicles and protected supply contracts. It favours sovereign land power and dependable series over cheaper imports or a wider European division of work.
descriptions.armament_gaullist_a_followup: A steady order book lets French plants preserve skilled teams and carry a vehicle line through successive improvements. The advantage comes from keeping one design in production long enough for workers and suppliers to master it; the cost is less flexibility when requirements change. This continuation puts the army's armoured fleet ahead of short runs across several competing equipment types.
descriptions.armament_gaullist_b: European aircraft cooperation can spread the cost of advanced design while keeping French engineers inside the programme. This route builds shared airframe standards and a trained technical workforce, drawing on the industrial logic that produced Airbus. Partners gain a voice in workshare and export choices, however, so France trades some unilateral control for a broader base of skills and production.
descriptions.armament_gaullist_b_followup: Common components and tooling allow French and partner plants to supply a shared airframe with fewer duplicated processes. The arrangement raises civilian productivity as expertise moves across the industrial network, but it also deepens exposure to outside decisions and supply interruptions. France retains its command authority while accepting that a cooperative aircraft programme cannot be directed from Paris alone.
descriptions.armament_orthodox_gaullist_a: France's strategic deterrent depends on a national industrial base, trained naval crews and the ability to maintain its submarines at home. This programme gives the naval arsenals priority and protects the continuity of undersea design expertise. Dockyard investment and specialist schools are costly commitments; land factories must wait while the force de frappe remains credible and under French command.
descriptions.armament_orthodox_gaullist_a_followup: The undersea fleet requires engineering knowledge that cannot be assembled only when a refit is due. Continuous design work and naval education preserve the cadres who keep French submarines and their support systems serviceable. The commitment strengthens national command at sea, but its long training horizon and public cost leave fewer resources for immediate conventional procurement.
descriptions.armament_orthodox_gaullist_b: A sovereign land force needs a domestic source of armoured vehicles and the ability to replace equipment without waiting on foreign permission. This route concentrates state support on French tank production and the industrial capacity behind it. The approach improves supply security, but it commits capital to a heavy fleet and leaves France bearing the full cost of design, orders and maintenance.
descriptions.armament_orthodox_gaullist_b_followup: French command vehicles, radios and mobile support units link dispersed formations to national headquarters. Standardizing these systems improves field coordination and reduces logistical strain, while their electrical demands press on the military-industrial base. The policy reinforces independent operations without placing French units under an allied command, but requires long-term procurement and technical support at home.
descriptions.armament_liberal_a: Independent aircraft firms and export contracts can reward engineering quality, provided the state gives manufacturers room to compete. This programme backs performance-based contracts and a stable airframe series, accepting lower corporate receipts in exchange for stronger industrial incentives. French firms gain commercial freedom, while the government must tolerate uneven results and the risk that export priorities shape domestic production choices.
descriptions.armament_liberal_a_followup: Export certification and advanced avionics help French aircraft meet demanding foreign standards and keep design teams close to the latest systems. This route invests in technical education and air doctrine rather than expanding every production line. The return depends on sustained research and access to overseas markets; a downturn in orders would leave the state carrying the cost of specialized expertise.
descriptions.armament_liberal_b: Replacing equipment less often can preserve public funds for training, maintenance and other national priorities. This route accepts a smaller arms-industrial footprint in exchange for lower equipment costs and longer service lives. It suits a government wary of permanent procurement growth, though a sudden crisis would expose the limits of an older inventory and the reduced capacity to surge new production.
descriptions.armament_liberal_b_followup: Shared maintenance fleets let military and civilian operators rely on common utility vehicles and familiar repair procedures. Standard parts reduce supply burdens and keep equipment useful longer, while careful production planning prevents depots from becoming a substitute for all new investment. The policy favors sustainment over expansion and asks France to accept slower modernization in return for lower recurring costs.
descriptions.armament_centre_a: Regional suppliers can keep army vehicles available without requiring every part to come from a single national contractor. This compact spreads orders among French workshops and firms, supporting local employment and a responsive supply chain. Tax concessions make participation attractive, but smaller suppliers need common specifications and dependable contracts or the dispersed network will struggle to meet military demand.
descriptions.armament_centre_a_followup: Common depot standards give units and regional workshops a shared language for inspecting, repairing and resupplying vehicles. Investment in training pays off in lower field consumption and more dependable service, though certification takes time and public support. The policy strengthens the army's reach through compatible local capacity rather than concentrating every repair decision in a central arsenal.
descriptions.armament_centre_b: France's Atlantic and Mediterranean commitments depend on ships that can be built and maintained by its own dockyards. This route directs industrial effort toward escort vessels and naval infrastructure, accepting slower growth in land-armament output. It offers maritime presence and secure sea lines, but a shipyard programme ties up capital for years before new hulls can enter service.
descriptions.armament_centre_b_followup: Fleet readiness rests on trained crews, regular exercises and refit schedules that keep ships available between deployments. This programme invests in naval doctrine and specialist education rather than simply increasing the number of hulls. Training improves coordination over time, but it is expensive and competes with immediate construction; the navy gains competence before it gains additional ships.
descriptions.armament_radical_a: The Republic's engineering schools and test establishments can improve military equipment without making procurement an extension of any single manufacturer. Open trials invite competing designs and publish technical requirements to a wider field of French expertise. The result may be better suited to public needs, but research takes time and its benefits arrive before any clear increase in the production line.
descriptions.armament_radical_a_followup: Independent test establishments let engineers compare communications equipment against operational needs rather than a supplier's claims. Shared evidence can improve doctrine and purchasing decisions, yet the testing apparatus consumes funds and can delay orders while designs are evaluated. The programme strengthens civilian oversight of technical choices and accepts slower arms-factory expansion as the price of scrutiny.
descriptions.armament_radical_b: Territorial units need affordable rifles and dependable equipment more than a prestige arsenal. This budget gives priority to basic infantry supply and lower purchase costs, while accepting a smaller production programme. It supports a broad defensive establishment and parliamentary control of expenditure, but France will have less capacity to rapidly enlarge its arms factories during a crisis.
descriptions.armament_radical_b_followup: Regional repair shops and shared utility vehicles allow local authorities to restore roads and move supplies after disruption. The arrangement links civil engineering to territorial readiness, while requiring public contracts and a stable network of small firms. It improves resilience outside major industrial centres, but each locality must maintain standards and equipment rather than relying on one central depot.
descriptions.armament_socialist_a: Public aerospace investment can preserve French design teams while making technical training part of the national industrial programme. The route favors advanced aircraft and research capacity over an immediate expansion of every armaments line. Long-term jobs and engineering skills strengthen the sector, but laboratories, apprenticeships and public contracts require sustained spending before the resulting aircraft can be fielded.
descriptions.armament_socialist_a_followup: Stable public orders protect specialist jobs through changes in the procurement cycle and give workers a stake in how new systems are built. The policy binds technical employment to social guarantees, raising the cost of the programme when production slows. It keeps skilled teams available for future aerospace work but leaves less fiscal room for rapid cuts or a sudden shift in priorities.
descriptions.armament_socialist_b: Conversion guarantees help armaments workers and suppliers move toward civilian production when defence orders recede. Public contracts support the transition, while reduced priority for arms output acknowledges that factories cannot serve every purpose at once. The policy preserves productive skills and social protections, but it limits the state's ability to expand military production quickly if the European balance deteriorates.
descriptions.armament_socialist_b_followup: A smaller fleet of durable utility vehicles gives the army dependable transport without making constant replacement the measure of readiness. Lower equipment costs preserve room for training and social spending, while technical schools maintain the skills needed to operate and repair the fleet. France accepts a slower modernization cycle in exchange for a force better matched to a negotiated social settlement.
descriptions.armament_communist_a: A public armaments plan coordinates orders, materials and labour across France's nationalized industrial base. Long series lower unit costs and give the state a reliable supply of infantry weapons, but heavy production draws electricity and inputs away from civilian users. The programme treats defence as a planned public service and asks factories to follow national priorities rather than local commercial returns.
descriptions.armament_communist_a_followup: Standardized production runs help public plants make equipment that units can maintain and replace without proliferating incompatible designs. Repetition builds capacity, though the system can be slow to absorb new requirements once plans and tooling are fixed. The policy favors predictable supply and common command equipment over experimental variety, reinforcing a centralized approach to procurement.
descriptions.armament_communist_b: Autonomous arsenal councils give workers and engineers a voice in maintenance priorities and local production decisions. Repair becomes a public responsibility shared by the people who know the equipment, rather than a distant administrative target. This flexibility can keep vehicles in service, but it may sacrifice the consistency and peak efficiency achieved by a single national production schedule.
descriptions.armament_communist_b_followup: Regional prototype workshops let technical teams test improvements close to the plants and units that will use them. Public education and applied engineering give local initiative a durable base, though experiments compete with predictable mass orders for skilled workers. The route values practical invention and repair over uniformity, accepting that not every workshop will deliver the same result.
descriptions.armament_old_guard_a: In this counterfactual hard-line programme, a central directorate assigns materials and production targets to state arsenals. Priority orders expand infantry equipment and the state's control over output, while civilian factories lose access to some resources. Central planning can sustain mass production in a crisis, but its rigid allocations leave less room for local adaptation and civilian investment.
descriptions.armament_old_guard_a_followup: Mobilisation schedules synchronize state plants around large, repeatable orders. Keeping factories on a common timetable raises the ceiling for wartime output, but lower flexibility makes it harder to change a series when field needs shift. This is an alternate-history extension of centralized planning, not a documented separate Old Guard platform or the later PCF's official line.
descriptions.armament_old_guard_b: Domestic repair establishments reduce dependence on imported components and preserve equipment through disciplined maintenance. The state directs resources toward workshops rather than new factory construction, lowering replacement costs but slowing the pace at which France can enlarge its arsenal. This counterfactual Old Guard policy prizes endurance and supply sovereignty over rapid modernization or a broader civilian industrial base.
descriptions.armament_old_guard_b_followup: National transport tooling keeps utility vehicles and military supply routes compatible across depots and production sites. Standardized mobility improves logistics and reduces consumption, though factories must devote energy to the system and leave less for other work. The programme strengthens central coordination without assigning French formations to foreign command; its ideological framing remains an explicit alternate-history proposal.
descriptions.armament_psu_a: Worker-managed suppliers let shop-floor councils shape production schedules and maintenance decisions for the equipment they build. More capable production teams improve reliability, though output becomes less uniform when each workshop has a voice in priorities. The programme applies PSU self-management to defence industries as a governing extrapolation, balancing workers' control against the army's need for dependable common equipment.
descriptions.armament_psu_a_followup: Cooperative maintenance networks bring public depots, local authorities and worker-run firms into a shared repair system. Lower replacement demands protect social budgets, while service guarantees require continued negotiation and public support. The approach favors keeping equipment useful over ordering new fleets, and tests whether decentralized cooperation can meet military standards without restoring a single command bureaucracy.
descriptions.armament_psu_b: Dual-use conversion moves engineering effort from weapons contracts toward transport, infrastructure and civilian machinery. Better civilian productivity comes at the cost of lower arms output, making this a real choice about the direction of public investment. The route extends the PSU's self-management principles into a plausible government policy; it is not presented as a settled military doctrine of the party in 1970.
descriptions.armament_psu_b_followup: Civilian technical institutes train engineers for energy, transport and industrial conversion, with skills that can also support territorial resilience. Their public mandate widens access to expertise but competes with military schools for funding and instructors. The policy favors a flexible technical workforce over narrow procurement specialization, accepting that defence modernization may proceed more slowly.
descriptions.armament_ecology_a: Civilian workshop conversion directs maintenance skills toward transport, infrastructure and emergency services instead of enlarging arms production. Existing French industrial expertise remains useful, but factories must adapt their tooling and retrain workers before civilian orders can replace defence contracts. This proposed ecological programme improves repair capacity while accepting a smaller military-industrial base; it does not claim the movement had a detailed historical defence platform.
descriptions.armament_ecology_a_followup: Civil-protection instrumentation equips engineers to monitor energy use, infrastructure failures and emergency conditions. Lower electricity demand and technical training support resilience without assuming that ecological politics automatically rejects France's deterrent. The investment competes with arms procurement and requires reliable public standards; it is a plausible policy for an ecological government, not a documented movement-wide military programme.
descriptions.armament_ecology_b: Retaining a limited set of defence workshops preserves repair skills and basic infantry supply while resisting a costly production surge. The programme lowers upkeep through simpler equipment and restrained factory growth, leaving the state less able to replace losses quickly. This is an ecological governing proposal for keeping territorial defence credible within industrial limits, not evidence of an established party doctrine.
descriptions.armament_ecology_b_followup: Service-life engineering extends the use of utility vehicles through careful maintenance, simpler components and lower supply demands. Production planning sacrifices some peak output to keep equipment serviceable for longer. The policy supports a smaller material footprint and robust local repair, but modernization takes place incrementally and depends on technical schools willing to prioritize maintenance over new designs.
descriptions.armament_cid_a: The CID's small traders and artisans can supply specialist repairs without building a large state contractor. This proposal uses independent workshops to lower equipment costs and retain local skills, with tax concessions reducing public revenue. It is an extrapolation from the movement's small-business constituency, not a historical CID defence programme; dispersed contracts require careful standards and can be difficult to coordinate.
descriptions.armament_cid_a_followup: Credit for workshop tooling helps local firms repair infrastructure and military utility vehicles with equipment they could not otherwise afford. Regional capacity grows, but uneven production standards and limited order books constrain efficiency. This proposed small-enterprise route gives the CID a plausible defence-industrial policy without attributing one to the historical movement; its success depends on voluntary contracts and reliable inspection.
descriptions.armament_cid_b: Small suppliers can make infantry equipment for public procurement while preserving the independence of local firms. The programme spreads arms orders across workshops rather than concentrating them in a state arsenal, but tax concessions reduce the state's return and fragmented capacity limits surge production. This is a counterfactual extension of the CID's independent-trader base, with coordination costs built into the choice.
descriptions.armament_cid_b_followup: Interchangeable local components make equipment easier to repair across a dispersed supplier network. Common specifications and technical instruction help small firms serve multiple depots, though they require public coordination and continuing contracts. The proposal trades the concentration of a large arsenal for locally held capacity; it imagines a CID government policy rather than claiming a documented defence platform.
descriptions.armament_national_a: A national sourcing rule directs procurement toward French suppliers and protects essential inputs from external pressure. Domestic contracts strengthen supply resilience but make equipment more expensive and narrow the pool of available designs. This proposed National Front policy reflects national-preference rhetoric without inventing a historical procurement doctrine; it gives France greater control at the price of weaker commercial access abroad.
descriptions.armament_national_a_followup: Protected domestic assembly keeps French workers and suppliers responsible for completing equipment at home. Longer production series improve consistency, while trade partners may object to a policy that favors national firms. This route treats assembly capacity as a matter of sovereignty, but reduced commercial goodwill makes future export cooperation and foreign component access less certain.
descriptions.armament_national_b: Intergovernmental production standards allow France to cooperate on technical requirements without surrendering national command. Training and compatible communications equipment help coordinate procurement, although reliance on outside standards can increase foreign influence over future choices. This is a proposed pragmatic alternative to strict national sourcing, not evidence that the National Front historically endorsed a specific military alliance or shared doctrine.
descriptions.armament_national_b_followup: Coordinated vehicle tooling and common utility specifications make logistics simpler when French units work alongside partners. Lower supply needs are useful, but shared designs demand continuing commercial relationships and tax concessions for domestic firms. The policy accepts limited interdependence in exchange for dependable mobility, while retaining French authority over deployments and refusing to assume any foreign government's consent in advance.
